content: Clinical trials are recognized as a critical component of a robust, country-driven R&D framework. However, challenges such as excessive bureaucracy, uncoordinated approval processes, and the absence of supportive environments hinder progress in many countries, delaying access to life-saving innovations. The guidance highlights the need for reforms to address these barriers and improve the quality, efficiency, and coordination of clinical trials globally. It focuses on public health priorities, particularly in underrepresented populations such as children, pregnant women, and older adults. Key recommendations include adopting risk-based and proportionate approaches to trial oversight, moving away from a one-size-fits-all model. For the first time, WHO provides practical guidance to assist national health authorities, regulatory bodies, funders, and other stakeholders in facilitating clinical trials and generating evidence on health interventions. Sustained domestic support and resources are deemed essential for financing these reforms. The guidance also underscores the importance of meeting long-standing recommendations, such as allocating at least 2% of health budgets to science and R&D and 5% of health-related development assistance to research. Countries prioritizing a reformed clinical research ecosystem, with input from public, private, and community stakeholders, stand to benefit significantly. These benefits include improved public trust, better locally derived evidence for clinical and public health decisions, enhanced health outcomes, faster access to tailored medical innovations, and progress toward health-related sustainable development goals (SDGs). Additionally, such reforms contribute to national resilience, economic productivity, and a thriving science and innovation ecosystem. WHO remains committed to supporting countries in applying this guidance to reform and streamline their clinical trial oversight and approval processes. The guidance was developed through extensive consultations with stakeholders, including member states, research funders, national health authorities, ethics committees, and civil society organizations. Feedback was gathered through public consultations, global surveys, and in-person meetings held in various regions. The final document integrates input from nearly 3,000 participants worldwide and reflects the collective expertise of technical advisory groups, academic institutions, and international organizations. The scope of the guidance encompasses all aspects of clinical trials, including planning, conduct, analysis, oversight, and funding. It focuses on randomized clinical trials (RCTs) but also addresses other trial designs and interventions, ranging from pharmaceutical medicines and vaccines to behavioral, digital, and public health approaches. The guidance aims to complement existing ethical and scientific standards while addressing the unique needs of underrepresented populations and resource-limited settings. In summary, this WHO guidance provides a roadmap for improving clinical trial ecosystems globally, ensuring they are ethical, efficient, and capable of generating high-quality evidence to advance public health.
